name: Linear Search
definition: Linear Search is the simplest searching algorithm that sequentially checks each element in a list until the target element is found or the list ends. It works on both sorted and unsorted arrays by comparing each element one by one with the key. No preprocessing of the data is required.
applications: Searching in small or unsorted datasets
Finding an element in a linked list
Verifying presence of an item in a list
key_points: Works on unsorted arrays
Simple to implement but inefficient for large datasets
O(1) best case when the element is at the first position
visual_description: Show a horizontal array of boxes with numbers. An arrow labeled 'key=8' points downward and slides from left to right, highlighting each box in sequence. When it reaches the box containing 8, it glows green. Indices 0 to n-1 are labeled below each box.

name: Binary Search
definition: Binary Search is an efficient algorithm for finding an item from a sorted list of items. It works by repeatedly dividing in half the portion of the list that could contain the item, until you've narrowed down the possible locations to just one.
applications: Finding a word in a dictionary
Debugging (finding where a bug was introduced)
key_points: Only works on sorted arrays
O(log n) time complexity
Divide and conquer approach

name: Jump Search
definition: Jump Search works on sorted arrays by jumping ahead by fixed steps (√n) instead of checking every element. After finding the interval where the element may lie, it performs a linear search within that block. It is faster than linear search and simpler than binary search in implementation.
applications: Systems where backward traversal is costly
key_points: Optimal jump size is √n
Array must be sorted
Combines jumping and linear search for efficiency
visual_description: Show a sorted array with blocks of √n elements each separated by dotted vertical lines. Arrows jump forward from block start to block start. When the right block is found, a smaller arrow does a linear scan within that block until the target is highlighted green.

name: Exponential Search
definition: Exponential Search finds the range where the target element lies by doubling the index (1, 2, 4, 8, ...) and then applies binary search within that range. It is especially useful for unbounded or infinite sorted arrays. The algorithm is very efficient when the target is near the beginning of the array.
applications: Online search problems where array size is unknown
Searching in sorted streams of data
key_points: Doubles the index range each step
Uses binary search after range is found
Optimal when element is near the start of the array
visual_description: Show a sorted array with an arrow jumping to positions 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 with exponentially growing leap labels. When the jump overshoots the target, highlight the range [i/2, i] in yellow and show a binary search narrowing down within that range to the target in green.

name: Bubble Sort
definition: Bubble Sort is a simple comparison-based sorting algorithm that repeatedly steps through the list and swaps adjacent elements if they are in the wrong order. Each pass moves the largest unsorted element to its correct position at the end. The algorithm gets its name from how smaller elements slowly 'bubble' to the top.
applications: Detecting nearly sorted arrays with optimized version
key_points: In-place sorting algorithm
Stable sort — preserves relative order of equal elements
Optimized with a 'swapped' flag to stop early if sorted
visual_description: Show an array with colored bars of varying heights. Use red arrows to show two adjacent bars being compared, and animated swapping when out of order. After each pass, shade the rightmost sorted elements in green. Show multiple passes until all bars are sorted and fully green.

name: Selection Sort
definition: Selection Sort divides the array into a sorted and unsorted region. In each pass, it finds the minimum element from the unsorted region and places it at the beginning of that region. This process repeats until the entire array is sorted.
applications: Sorting small arrays with minimal memory
Sorting when write operations are expensive
key_points: Always performs O(n²) comparisons regardless of input
Makes at most n-1 swaps, fewer than bubble sort
Not stable — may change relative order of equal elements
visual_description: Show an array split into a green sorted region on the left and a white unsorted region on the right. A magnifying glass scans the unsorted portion to find the minimum element (highlighted red), then an arrow shows it swapping to the first unsorted position. Repeat until all green.

name: Insertion Sort
definition: Insertion Sort builds the sorted array one element at a time by picking each element and inserting it into its correct position among the already sorted elements. It is similar to how people sort playing cards in their hands. It is efficient for small datasets and nearly sorted arrays.
applications: Sorting small or nearly sorted arrays
Online algorithms where data arrives one at a time
Used as a base case in hybrid sorts like Timsort
key_points: Stable and in-place sorting algorithm
Best case O(n) when the array is already sorted
Adaptive — performs fewer operations on nearly sorted arrays
visual_description: Show a hand of playing cards. Each new card (highlighted) is picked from the unsorted right side and inserted in the correct position among sorted cards on the left. Use arrows shifting existing cards right to make space, then slot the new card in. Repeat for each card.

name: Merge Sort
definition: Merge Sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that splits the array into halves, recursively sorts each half, and then merges the two sorted halves into a single sorted array. It guarantees O(n log n) performance in all cases. It is particularly effective for sorting linked lists and large datasets.
key_points: Stable sort with guaranteed O(n log n) time
Requires O(n) extra space for merging
Based on divide-and-conquer paradigm
visual_description: Show a tree diagram. The root holds the full array split into two halves at the first level, then four quarters, down to single elements at the leaves. Arrows going back up show two sorted arrays being merged into one. Color sorted segments green as they merge upward.

name: Quick Sort
definition: Quick Sort is a highly efficient divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm that selects a 'pivot' element and partitions the array into elements less than and greater than the pivot. It recursively sorts both partitions. Despite an O(n²) worst case, its average performance and cache efficiency make it one of the fastest practical sorting algorithms.
applications: General-purpose sorting in most standard libraries
Sorting arrays with good cache performance
key_points: In-place sort with O(log n) stack space
Worst case O(n²) occurs with poor pivot selection
Randomized pivot selection improves average performance
visual_description: Show an array with the last element highlighted as pivot. Use blue shading for elements less than pivot and red for greater. Show a partition step with two pointers moving inward, then the pivot placed in its final correct position in green. Show recursive sub-arrays branching below.

name: Heap Sort
definition: Heap Sort uses a binary heap data structure to sort elements. It first builds a max-heap from the array, then repeatedly extracts the maximum element (root) and places it at the end of the array, reducing the heap size by one each time. It is an in-place, non-stable sorting algorithm with consistent O(n log n) performance.
applications: Systems requiring guaranteed O(n log n) sorting
key_points: In-place sorting with O(1) extra space
Not stable — may reorder equal elements
First phase builds a max-heap in O(n) time
visual_description: Show a binary tree representation of the array as a max-heap, with each parent larger than its children. Highlight the root (max), then show it swapping with the last leaf (which turns green as sorted). Re-heapify the reduced tree. Repeat until only the root remains and all nodes are green.

name: Counting Sort
definition: Counting Sort is a non-comparison-based sorting algorithm that sorts integers by counting the occurrences of each distinct value. It creates a count array, computes cumulative counts, and uses them to place elements in the correct output position. It is extremely fast when the range of input values is small relative to the number of elements.
applications: Sorting integers with a known limited range
Used as a subroutine in Radix Sort
key_points: Not comparison-based — beats O(n log n) lower bound
Efficient only when k (max value) is not much larger than n
Stable sort when implemented correctly
visual_description: Show three rows: the original array, a count array indexed 0 to max showing frequency bars for each value, and a cumulative count array. Arrows then map from cumulative counts to positions in the output array, filling elements from right to left to maintain stability.

name: Radix Sort
definition: Radix Sort is a non-comparison sorting algorithm that sorts integers digit by digit, from the least significant digit to the most significant digit, using a stable sort (like Counting Sort) as a subroutine. It processes each digit position independently, resulting in a sorted array after processing all digit positions.
applications: Sorting IP addresses or phone numbers
key_points: Processes digit by digit using a stable sub-sort
k is the number of digits in the maximum number
Not comparison-based — can outperform comparison sorts
visual_description: Show three passes for a list of 3-digit numbers. In each pass, label which digit position is being sorted (ones, tens, hundreds). Show ten buckets (0–9) per pass where numbers fall into, then concatenate them. After all three passes, the array is fully sorted and highlighted green.

name: Array
definition: An Array is a collection of elements stored at contiguous memory locations, all of the same data type. Elements can be accessed directly using their index in O(1) time. Arrays are the most fundamental data structure and form the building blocks for many other data structures.
applications: Implementing other data structures like stacks and queues
key_points: Fixed size once declared in C
O(1) random access using index
Insertion and deletion in the middle require shifting elements — O(n)
visual_description: Show a row of equally sized boxes labeled index 0 to n-1 below each box. Each box contains a number. A pointer labeled 'arr' points to the first box. Show memory addresses increasing from left to right below the boxes, illustrating contiguous memory allocation.

name: Linked List (Singly)
definition: A Singly Linked List is a linear data structure where each element (node) contains a data field and a pointer to the next node in the sequence. Unlike arrays, nodes are not stored in contiguous memory. Insertion and deletion at the head are O(1), but random access requires traversal from the head.
key_points: Dynamic size — no need to define size beforehand
No random access — must traverse from head
Efficient insertion and deletion at the head O(1)
visual_description: Show a chain of rectangular nodes each split into two sections: left for data and right for a pointer. Arrows connect the pointer section of each node to the data section of the next. The last node's pointer points to NULL. A 'HEAD' label with an arrow points to the first node.

name: Doubly Linked List
definition: A Doubly Linked List is a linked list where each node has two pointers: one pointing to the next node and another pointing to the previous node. This bidirectional linkage allows traversal in both directions. It enables O(1) deletion of a given node if its pointer is known, unlike a singly linked list.
key_points: Each node stores two pointers — uses more memory than singly linked list
Traversal in both directions is possible
O(1) deletion if node pointer is given directly
visual_description: Show a chain of nodes each with three sections: a left arrow (prev), center data, right arrow (next). Double-headed arrows connect neighboring nodes. The first node's prev points to NULL and the last node's next points to NULL. HEAD and TAIL labels mark the ends.

name: Stack
definition: A Stack is a linear data structure that follows the Last In, First Out (LIFO) principle. Elements are added (push) and removed (pop) from the same end called the 'top'. It is analogous to a stack of plates where you can only add or remove from the top.
key_points: LIFO order — last element inserted is first removed
Push, pop, and peek are all O(1) operations
Can be implemented with arrays or linked lists
visual_description: Show a vertical stack of boxes growing upward. A 'TOP' arrow points to the topmost filled box. Show a PUSH operation adding a new box on top (with a downward arrow) and a POP operation removing the top box (with an upward arrow). Label the LIFO principle clearly.

name: Queue
definition: A Queue is a linear data structure that follows the First In, First Out (FIFO) principle. Elements are added at the rear (enqueue) and removed from the front (dequeue). It models real-world queues like waiting lines.
key_points: FIFO order — first element in is first removed
Enqueue at rear, dequeue from front
Can be implemented with arrays or linked lists
visual_description: Show a horizontal row of boxes. An arrow labeled 'ENQUEUE' points into the right (REAR) end adding a new box. Another arrow labeled 'DEQUEUE' points out of the left (FRONT) end removing a box. Elements are labeled in order. FRONT and REAR pointers are shown above the respective ends.

name: Circular Queue
definition: A Circular Queue is a linear data structure that connects the last position back to the first, forming a circle. It overcomes the limitation of a simple array-based queue where space is wasted after dequeuing. The front and rear pointers wrap around using modular arithmetic.
key_points: Uses modular arithmetic to wrap around the array
Solves the 'false overflow' problem of linear queue
Full condition: (rear + 1) % MAX == front
visual_description: Show a circular arrangement of numbered boxes forming a ring. FRONT and REAR pointers are shown as arrows on the circle. Highlight elements between FRONT and REAR in blue. Show an enqueue adding at REAR (moves clockwise) and a dequeue removing at FRONT (moves clockwise). Use an arrow looping from last to first box.

name: Priority Queue
definition: A Priority Queue is an abstract data type where each element has a priority and elements are dequeued in order of their priority rather than insertion order. It is typically implemented using a binary heap. The highest (or lowest) priority element is always at the front.
key_points: Implemented efficiently with a binary heap
Insert and extract-max are O(log n)
Can be min-priority or max-priority depending on use case
visual_description: Show a binary heap tree with the maximum value at the root highlighted in gold. Show child nodes with smaller values below. An INSERT arrow shows a new value bubbling up from a leaf to its correct position. An EXTRACT-MAX arrow shows the root being removed and the heap restructuring (heapify down).

name: Hash Table
definition: A Hash Table is a data structure that maps keys to values using a hash function to compute an index (bucket) in an array. It provides near-constant time average-case lookup, insertion, and deletion. Collisions, where two keys hash to the same index, are handled via chaining or open addressing.
key_points: Hash function determines the bucket index
Collisions resolved by chaining (linked list at each bucket)
Worst case O(n) when all keys collide into one bucket
visual_description: Show a vertical array of buckets labeled 0 to TABLE_SIZE-1. Arrows from key values (labeled with the hash function formula) point to their respective buckets. Buckets with multiple elements show a short linked list chain horizontally. Highlight one key being looked up by following its hash arrow to its bucket.

name: Binary Tree
definition: A Binary Tree is a hierarchical data structure where each node has at most two children, referred to as the left child and the right child. The topmost node is called the root. Binary trees are the foundation for many advanced tree-based data structures and algorithms.
applications: Building binary search trees and heaps
key_points: Each node has at most 2 children
Height of tree determines performance
Degenerate (skewed) tree degrades to O(n) operations
visual_description: Show a tree diagram with a root node at the top, two children at the next level, and further children below forming a pyramid shape. Label each node with a number. Draw edges connecting parents to left and right children. Mark NULL pointers at leaf children as empty boxes or diagonal slashes.

name: Binary Search Tree (BST)
definition: A Binary Search Tree is a binary tree with the property that for every node, all values in the left subtree are less than the node's value and all values in the right subtree are greater. This ordering property makes search, insertion, and deletion efficient on average. Inorder traversal of a BST yields sorted output.
key_points: Left subtree < root < right subtree
Worst case O(n) when tree is skewed (degenerate)
Inorder traversal gives sorted sequence
visual_description: Show a BST with root 50. Left subtree has 30 with children 20 and 40. Right subtree has 70 with children 60 and 80. Label each edge with 'less than' or 'greater than'. Show a search for 40 by tracing the path: root→30→40, highlighting each visited node in yellow until the target is found in green.

name: AVL Tree
definition: A self-balancing Binary Search Tree where the heights of two child subtrees differ by at most one.
key_points: Self-balancing
Balance factor = -1,0,1
Rotations for balancing

name: Graph (Adjacency List)
definition: A Graph is a non-linear data structure consisting of vertices (nodes) and edges (connections). An Adjacency List represents a graph where each vertex stores a list of its neighboring vertices. This is space-efficient for sparse graphs, using O(V + E) space compared to O(V²) for an adjacency matrix.
key_points: Space-efficient for sparse graphs O(V + E)
Adding an edge is O(1)
Checking if an edge exists is O(degree) not O(1)
visual_description: Show a vertical array of vertices 0 to V-1 on the left side. Each vertex has a horizontal linked list extending to the right, containing the indices of its neighbors as node boxes with arrows. Show edges in the graph diagram above, with matching color connections linking to corresponding list entries.

name: Tree Traversal (Inorder)
definition: Inorder Traversal visits nodes in the order: Left subtree → Root → Right subtree. For a Binary Search Tree, this traversal yields nodes in ascending sorted order. It is a depth-first traversal that uses recursion or a stack.
applications: Printing BST elements in sorted order
key_points: Left → Root → Right visit order
Produces sorted output for BSTs
Recursion depth equals the height of the tree
visual_description: Show a binary tree with nodes numbered. Draw a dashed traversal path that first dives deep into the left subtree, then visits the root, then the right subtree. Number each node visit in sequence (1, 2, 3...) with small red circles. Highlight nodes turning green as they are visited in Left-Root-Right order.

name: Tree Traversal (Preorder)
definition: Preorder Traversal visits nodes in the order: Root → Left subtree → Right subtree. The root is processed before its children, making this traversal useful for creating a copy of the tree or serializing its structure. It is a depth-first traversal.
applications: Prefix expression generation from expression trees
key_points: Root → Left → Right visit order
First node visited is always the root
Used to reconstruct a tree from its traversal
visual_description: Show a binary tree. Draw a dashed traversal path that starts at the root (visited first, marked 1), then goes left to the left subtree root (marked 2), continues down left, then backtracks up and right. Number each node in the visit sequence. Highlight each node green as it is visited in Root-Left-Right order.

name: Tree Traversal (Postorder)
definition: Postorder Traversal visits nodes in the order: Left subtree → Right subtree → Root. The root is processed after all its descendants, making it ideal for deleting a tree or evaluating postfix expressions. It is a depth-first traversal.
applications: Deleting a tree safely (children before parent)
Computing directory sizes (children before parent folder)
key_points: Left → Right → Root visit order
Root is always visited last
Safe for deletion since children are processed first
visual_description: Show a binary tree. Draw a dashed traversal path that first goes all the way down to leaves in the left subtree (visited first), then right subtree leaves, then back up to parent nodes. Number each node visit in sequence. The root node is numbered last. Highlight nodes green after being visited in Left-Right-Root order.

name: Level Order Traversal
definition: Level Order Traversal visits all nodes at the current depth (level) before moving to the next level, processing the tree from top to bottom and left to right. It uses a queue to track the next nodes to visit. This is also known as Breadth-First Search (BFS) for trees.
applications: Finding the shortest path in unweighted trees
Connecting nodes at the same level
key_points: Uses a queue — FIFO order drives level-by-level traversal
Visits all nodes at depth d before depth d+1
Space complexity O(n) due to queue holding up to one full level
visual_description: Show a tree with horizontal dashed lines separating Level 0 (root), Level 1, Level 2, etc. A horizontal queue at the bottom shows nodes being dequeued from the front (visited and printed) while their children are enqueued at the rear. Number nodes in the visit order 1, 2, 3... from left to right, level by level.

name: Breadth-First Search (BFS)
definition: BFS explores a graph level by level, visiting all neighbors of the current vertex before moving to the next level. It uses a queue and a visited array to avoid revisiting nodes. BFS finds the shortest path in unweighted graphs and is complete — it always finds a solution if one exists.
applications: Web crawling and social network analysis
Finding connected components in a graph
key_points: Uses a queue for FIFO traversal
Guarantees shortest path in unweighted graphs
Visited array prevents infinite loops in cyclic graphs
visual_description: Show a graph with labeled vertices. Starting from vertex 0, highlight it in green and add it to a queue at the bottom. Draw concentric rings around the start vertex showing Level 1 (direct neighbors), Level 2 (neighbors of neighbors), etc. Each visited vertex changes color from white to green as it is dequeued and processed.

name: Depth-First Search (DFS)
definition: DFS explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking. It uses a stack (or recursion) and a visited array. DFS is used for cycle detection, topological sort, and solving maze-like problems. Unlike BFS, it does not guarantee the shortest path.
key_points: Uses recursion or an explicit stack
Explores deep paths before backtracking
Does not guarantee shortest path unlike BFS
visual_description: Show a graph with labeled vertices. Starting at vertex 0, draw a deep path going through vertices in DFS order, using a thick colored line. When a dead-end is reached, show a backtrack arrow (dashed line going back) before exploring the next branch. Color each vertex as it is first visited. Show the call stack on the side growing and shrinking.

name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
definition: Dijkstra's Algorithm finds the shortest paths from a single source vertex to all other vertices in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. It uses a greedy approach, always expanding the vertex with the smallest known distance. A priority queue (min-heap) makes it efficient.
key_points: Only works with non-negative edge weights
Greedy algorithm — always picks the minimum cost vertex
Priority queue implementation gives O((V+E) log V) time
visual_description: Show a weighted graph. Mark the source node in gold. Display a table of tentative distances initialized to infinity. At each step, highlight the current vertex in green (minimum distance), show relaxation of its neighbors (update their distance if shorter), and mark settled vertices. Show the shortest path tree formed by bold edges at the end.

name: Bellman-Ford Algorithm
definition: Bellman-Ford computes shortest paths from a single source vertex in a weighted graph and handles negative edge weights, unlike Dijkstra's. It relaxes all edges V-1 times to guarantee shortest paths, and can detect negative weight cycles. The algorithm is slower than Dijkstra's but more versatile.
applications: Routing with negative cost links (e.g., currency arbitrage)
Detecting negative cycles in financial graphs
key_points: Handles negative edge weights (Dijkstra's cannot)
Runs V-1 relaxation passes over all edges
Detects negative weight cycles in the Vth pass
visual_description: Show a graph with edges labeled including one negative weight edge. Create a table showing dist[] values after each of V-1 rounds of relaxation. Highlight updated distances in yellow. After all passes, show a final check for negative cycles. Draw the final shortest path tree with bold colored edges.

name: Floyd-Warshall Algorithm
definition: Floyd-Warshall is a dynamic programming algorithm that finds shortest paths between all pairs of vertices in a weighted graph, including graphs with negative weights (but no negative cycles). It updates a distance matrix by considering each vertex as an intermediate node. It runs in O(V³) time.
applications: All-pairs shortest path in network routing
Finding transitive closure of a graph
key_points: Uses dynamic programming with V iterations
Works for directed graphs with negative weights
Space: O(V²) for the distance matrix
visual_description: Show a V×V distance matrix. Initially filled with direct edge weights and INF where no edge exists. Show three nested loop iterations where vertex k acts as an intermediate node. Highlight cells where dist[i][j] is updated (shortened) via k in blue. Show the final all-pairs shortest path matrix as the result.

name: Prim's Algorithm
definition: Prim's Algorithm finds the Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) of a connected weighted graph by starting from an arbitrary vertex and greedily adding the cheapest edge that connects a new vertex to the growing MST. It ensures all vertices are connected with minimum total edge weight.
applications: Laying out minimum cable for a network
Approximation algorithms for the Traveling Salesman Problem
key_points: Greedy algorithm growing the MST one vertex at a time
Uses a priority queue for efficiency
Differs from Kruskal's: grows from a single tree vs multiple components
visual_description: Show a weighted undirected graph. Highlight the starting vertex in gold. As the MST grows, color selected edges bold green and add newly joined vertices to the green MST region. At each step, show a priority queue of candidate edges with weights and highlight the minimum weight edge being selected. Show the final MST with all green edges and total weight.

name: Kruskal's Algorithm
definition: Kruskal's Algorithm builds a Minimum Spanning Tree by sorting all edges by weight and adding each edge to the MST if it does not form a cycle, using a Union-Find (Disjoint Set) data structure for cycle detection. It processes edges globally in weight order, unlike Prim's vertex-centric approach.
applications: Network design with minimum cabling cost
Connecting cities with minimum road cost
key_points: Edges are sorted by weight first
Union-Find detects and prevents cycles
Works well for sparse graphs where E << V²
visual_description: Show all graph edges sorted in a list by weight from top to bottom. Process each edge one at a time. If the edge's endpoints belong to different components (shown as separate colored groups), draw it as a bold green MST edge and merge the groups. If adding it would form a cycle, mark it red and skip it. Show the final MST with all green edges.

name: Topological Sort
definition: Topological Sort produces a linear ordering of vertices in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) such that for every directed edge u → v, vertex u appears before v in the ordering. It is based on DFS and uses a stack to record the finish order. Topological sort is undefined for graphs with cycles.
key_points: Only applicable to Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs)
DFS-based: vertices are pushed to stack after all descendants are visited
Kahn's algorithm (BFS-based) is an alternative approach
visual_description: Show a DAG with directed edges (arrows). Label each node with a course or task name. Draw a linear sequence at the bottom representing the topological order. Arrows from the DAG map to their position in the linear sequence. Show that for every edge u→v in the DAG, u always appears to the left of v in the sequence.

name: Fibonacci (Memoization)
definition: The Fibonacci sequence using memoization improves on naive recursion by storing the results of already-computed subproblems in a cache (array or hash map). When the same subproblem is encountered again, its result is retrieved from the cache in O(1) instead of recomputed. This is top-down dynamic programming.
key_points: Reduces time from O(2^n) exponential to O(n) linear
Cache stores results to avoid redundant computation
Top-down DP — uses recursion with a memo table
visual_description: Show a recursion tree for fib(5). In the naive version, mark many repeated subtrees (fib(3), fib(2)) in red. In the memoized version, show the same tree but with repeated nodes replaced by arrows pointing to a cached value table. Highlight cache hits in gold and new computations in blue.

name: Kadane's Algorithm
definition: Kadane's Algorithm finds the maximum sum subarray of a one-dimensional array in O(n) time using dynamic programming. It iterates through the array, keeping track of the maximum sum ending at the current position and the overall maximum found so far. It handles arrays with negative numbers elegantly.
applications: Finding the best performing time window in data
key_points: Solves maximum subarray problem in O(n)
Resets running sum to 0 when it becomes negative
Tracks start and end indices of the maximum subarray
visual_description: Show a horizontal array with positive values in blue and negative in red. Draw a sliding highlight over the current subarray being considered. Show two variables: 'maxEndingHere' (current sum) and 'maxSoFar' (global max) updating in real-time below the array. Highlight the final maximum subarray in bold green.

name: Longest Common Subsequence
definition: Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) finds the longest sequence that appears in both given strings in the same relative order but not necessarily contiguously. It uses a 2D DP table where each cell stores the LCS length for the corresponding prefixes. The result is found at the bottom-right cell of the table.
applications: Diff tools for comparing files (git diff)
key_points: 2D DP table of size (m+1) × (n+1)
Diagonal fill when characters match
Subsequence is not the same as substring — gaps are allowed
visual_description: Show a 2D grid with string X along the top and string Y along the left side. Fill each cell with the LCS length up to that prefix. Highlight cells where characters match in gold (diagonal fill). Trace back the optimal path from the bottom-right cell to the top-left to reconstruct the actual LCS, highlighting the path in green.

name: 0/1 Knapsack
definition: The 0/1 Knapsack problem asks for the maximum value that can be placed in a knapsack of limited weight capacity, given items each with a weight and value. Each item can either be taken (1) or left (0). It is solved using a 2D DP table where rows represent items and columns represent remaining capacities.
key_points: Each item is either fully included or excluded
DP table indexed by item count and remaining capacity
Traceback through the table reveals which items were selected
visual_description: Show a 2D DP table with items as rows (0 to n) and capacities as columns (0 to W). Fill cells row by row, highlighting in yellow when an item is included (diagonal lookup) vs. carried from above when excluded. Mark the maximum value cell in gold. Show an arrow traceback path from the bottom-right revealing which items were selected.

name: Coin Change Problem
definition: The Coin Change Problem finds the minimum number of coins needed to make a given amount using coins of given denominations. It uses a 1D DP array where each index represents an amount and stores the minimum coins needed. This is a classic unbounded knapsack variant.
key_points: Bottom-up DP filling amounts 1 to target
Each amount checks all coin denominations
Returns -1 if the amount cannot be made
visual_description: Show a 1D DP array indexed 0 to amount. Index 0 = 0 coins. For each subsequent index, show arrows from earlier indices (index - coin value) pointing forward, with the minimum value being selected. Highlight cells being filled in order. At the end, the cell at index 'amount' shows the minimum coin count in gold.

name: Naive Pattern Matching
definition: Naive Pattern Matching checks all possible positions in a text string where a pattern might occur by sliding the pattern one position at a time and comparing character by character. It requires no preprocessing but can be slow for large inputs. It serves as the baseline approach for more advanced pattern matching algorithms.
applications: Simple text search in small documents
key_points: Slides pattern one position at a time over text
No preprocessing required
Worst case O(nm) with repeated mismatches
visual_description: Show a long text string at the top and a shorter pattern below it. Show the pattern sliding under the text from left to right. At each position, highlight matching characters in green and the first mismatch in red. When all characters match, highlight the entire aligned section in gold. Show all found positions labeled below.

name: KMP Algorithm
definition: The Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm is an efficient pattern matching algorithm that preprocesses the pattern to build a failure function (partial match table), which tells how much to shift the pattern on a mismatch without re-examining already matched text characters. This achieves O(n + m) time complexity.
applications: Efficient text editors and search tools
key_points: LPS (Longest Proper Prefix Suffix) array prevents redundant comparisons
Never re-examines already matched text characters
Preprocessing the pattern takes O(m) time
visual_description: Show two sections: LPS table construction and the main search. For LPS, show the pattern with prefix-suffix matches highlighted. For the search, show the text on top and pattern below. On a mismatch, instead of shifting by 1, show the pattern jumping forward using the LPS value. Highlight matching sections in green and the mismatch position in red.

name: Rabin-Karp Algorithm
definition: Rabin-Karp uses hashing to find pattern occurrences in a text. It computes the hash of the pattern and a sliding window hash of the text, comparing hashes in O(1). When hashes match, a character-by-character check confirms the match to handle collisions (spurious hits). It is efficient for multiple pattern searching.
applications: Detecting duplicate content on the web
key_points: Rolling hash allows O(1) window hash updates
Spurious hits (hash collision) require verification
Excellent for searching multiple patterns simultaneously
visual_description: Show the text at the top with a sliding window of length m highlighted in blue. Below the window, show the computed hash value. Show the pattern hash value alongside. When hashes match, highlight the window in yellow and show character verification. When they mismatch, show the window sliding right and the hash updating with a rolling formula arrow.

name: Longest Palindromic Substring
definition: The Longest Palindromic Substring problem finds the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forward and backward. The expand-around-center approach treats each character (and gap between characters) as a potential palindrome center and expands outward while characters match. It runs in O(n²) time with O(1) space.
applications: DNA sequence analysis for repeated patterns
Text processing and natural language analysis
key_points: Two expansion types: odd-length (single center) and even-length (pair center)
Each center expands while left and right characters match
Manacher's algorithm can solve this in O(n)
visual_description: Show a string with characters in boxes. Highlight a center character in gold. Show two expansion arrows going outward left and right simultaneously. Color matched pairs in green as the palindrome expands. When characters stop matching, show the boundary. Repeat for all centers and highlight the longest found palindrome with a bold green bracket.

name: Sieve of Eratosthenes
definition: The Sieve of Eratosthenes is an ancient algorithm for finding all prime numbers up to a limit n. It starts by assuming all numbers are prime, then iteratively marks the multiples of each prime as composite, starting from 2. The unmarked numbers remaining after the process are all primes.
key_points: Only iterate up to √n for the outer loop
Start marking multiples from p² not 2p
One of the most efficient algorithms for finding all primes up to n
visual_description: Show a grid of numbers 2 to n. Mark 2 in gold (prime) and cross out all its multiples (4, 6, 8...) in red. Move to 3 (prime), cross out 9, 12, 15... Skip 4 (already crossed). Continue for each unmarked number. At the end, all uncrossed numbers are highlighted gold as primes. Show the grid progressively being filled with red crosses.

name: Euclidean Algorithm (GCD)
definition: The Euclidean Algorithm efficiently computes the Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) of two integers using the property that GCD(a, b) = GCD(b, a mod b). It repeatedly replaces the larger number with the remainder until the remainder is zero. The last non-zero remainder is the GCD.
key_points: Based on the property GCD(a, b) = GCD(b, a mod b)
Converges in O(log(min(a,b))) steps
One of the oldest algorithms in mathematics
visual_description: Show a step-by-step table with two columns: A and B. Each row shows the values of A and B and the remainder A mod B. Arrows indicate B becoming the new A and remainder becoming the new B. The final row where B=0 is highlighted in gold, with the GCD value pointed to by an arrow.

name: Fast Exponentiation
definition: Fast Exponentiation (Binary Exponentiation) computes x^n in O(log n) time by repeatedly squaring the base and using the binary representation of the exponent. If the current bit of n is 1, multiply the result by the current power of x. This avoids O(n) multiplications from naive repeated multiplication.
key_points: Reduces O(n) multiplications to O(log n)
Uses binary representation of the exponent
Essential for modular arithmetic in cryptography
visual_description: Show the binary representation of exponent n (e.g., 13 = 1101 in binary). For each bit from right to left, show two operations: squaring the base and conditionally multiplying the result. Draw a table with columns for bit position, current base value (squared each step), and the running result. Highlight bits that are '1' in gold.

name: Prime Number Check
definition: A prime number check determines whether a given number n is prime by testing divisibility. The optimized trial division only checks divisors up to √n, since any factor larger than √n would have a corresponding factor smaller than √n. Numbers 2 and 3 are special-cased, and even numbers are skipped after 2.
applications: Generating prime numbers for hash table sizing
key_points: Only check divisors up to √n
Skip even numbers after checking 2
Probabilistic tests (Miller-Rabin) used for very large numbers
visual_description: Show a number line from 1 to n. Mark 1 as neither prime nor composite. Show divisor checks starting from 2 up to √n. For each divisor tested, show a division operation. If remainder is 0 (divisible), highlight the number red (composite). If no divisors found, highlight green (prime). Show √n as a cutoff boundary on the number line.

name: Factorial (Recursive & Iterative)
definition: Factorial of a non-negative integer n (written n!) is the product of all positive integers from 1 to n, with 0! = 1 by definition. It can be computed recursively (n! = n × (n-1)!) or iteratively (using a loop). Factorial grows extremely fast and is fundamental in permutations, combinations, and probability.
key_points: Recursive version has O(n) call stack depth
Iterative version uses O(1) space
Overflows quickly — use long long or big integers for large n
visual_description: Show two side-by-side diagrams. Left: a recursive call stack for factorial(5) showing factorial(5)→factorial(4)→...→factorial(1) stacked vertically, then unwinding with return values multiplied. Right: an iterative loop diagram showing a result variable being multiplied by 2, 3, 4, 5 in sequence inside a loop box, with the final answer highlighted in gold.
